modules.title: Python foundations
modules.summary: Use variables, collections, loops and functions to turn a question into a repeatable calculation.
lesson: A list stores an ordered collection. A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Choose the structure that matches your data.
Write small functions with explicit inputs and outputs. Test the empty input and the usual case before working with a larger dataset.
tasks: Write a function that computes total revenue from a list of prices.
Handle an empty list and explain your return value.

modules.title: Explore and clean data
modules.summary: Inspect a table, find missing values and build a documented cleaning process.
lesson: Start by checking shape, column types, missing values and duplicate keys. A missing value can mean unknown, unavailable or not applicable.
Avoid filling every missing value with zero. Decide using the meaning of the column and document what changed.
tasks: Load a CSV and produce a missing-value summary.
Create a cleaned copy and document three decisions.

modules.title: SQL for analysis
modules.summary: Filter, aggregate and join tables without losing sight of the grain of your data.
lesson: The grain describes what one row represents. Confirm the grain before a join so that repeated keys do not silently multiply your totals.
WHERE filters rows before aggregation. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. COUNT(column) excludes nulls; COUNT(*) counts rows.
tasks: Calculate revenue by customer using GROUP BY.
Compare row counts before and after joining an orders table.

modules.title: Statistics that explain
modules.summary: Describe variation, compare groups and communicate uncertainty.
lesson: The mean is sensitive to extreme observations. The median is often a useful companion when a distribution is skewed.
Correlation describes association, not causation. Confounding variables and selection effects can explain an apparent relationship.
tasks: Compare mean and median for a skewed price column.
Describe one conclusion your dataset cannot support.

modules.title: Visual storytelling
modules.summary: Choose a chart that answers a question and write an evidence-based takeaway.
lesson: Use bars for category comparisons and lines for time trends. A scatter plot helps inspect relationships between numeric variables.
Label units and show the relevant baseline. Write a title that makes the question clear and avoid implying precision the data does not support.
tasks: Create one comparison chart and one trend chart.
Add a takeaway and a limitation below each chart.

modules.title: Advanced SQL patterns
modules.summary: Use CTEs and window functions for rankings, running totals and comparisons.
lesson: GROUP BY collapses rows; a window function calculates across related rows while retaining each row. PARTITION BY defines the groups for a window.
Use explicit ordering for running calculations. Ties behave differently in ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK.
tasks: Rank customers by revenue within each region.
Calculate a running total with an explicit window frame.

modules.title: Build a useful dashboard
modules.summary: Turn a business question into a small, readable dashboard with defined metrics.
lesson: Define each metric, its time range and the decision it supports before choosing visuals. A dashboard should help someone decide what to do next.
Check filter behaviour and reconcile totals against a source query. A visually polished dashboard can still be wrong.
tasks: Define revenue, order count and average order value.
Build a dashboard and reconcile its totals to SQL.

modules.title: Experiments and decisions
modules.summary: Frame a hypothesis, choose a metric and recognise the limits of an experiment.
lesson: Choose a primary outcome and success criterion before observing results. Random assignment helps reduce confounding.
Statistical significance is not the same as practical value. Consider effect size, uncertainty and the cost of implementation.
tasks: Draft an experiment for a checkout change.
Specify a primary metric and a guardrail metric.

modules.title: Features and validation
modules.summary: Create a reproducible train/test split and prevent leakage.
lesson: Split data before fitting transformations. A preprocessing step fitted on all observations can leak information from the test set into training.
Choose validation that matches the problem: chronological splits for future prediction and group-aware splits for repeated entities.
tasks: Create a held-out test set and a preprocessing pipeline.
Identify one potential source of leakage.

modules.title: Train a baseline model
modules.summary: Compare a simple baseline with a model and choose a relevant evaluation metric.
lesson: A baseline establishes whether added complexity helps. Compare against a simple rule such as predicting the majority class or the training mean.
Accuracy alone can mislead when classes are imbalanced. Examine precision, recall and the confusion matrix in the context of error costs.
tasks: Fit a dummy baseline and a tree-based model.
Compare their performance using the same validation split.

modules.title: Explain model behaviour
modules.summary: Inspect errors by segment and communicate where a model should not be trusted.
lesson: An overall metric can hide poor performance on a subgroup. Inspect errors across meaningful segments and document small sample sizes.
Feature importance is a description of a fitted model, not evidence that changing a feature will cause the outcome to change.
tasks: Review five false predictions and group common errors.
Write a model card with limitations and intended use.

modules.title: Publish your evidence
modules.summary: Present a reproducible project with a clear question, evidence and limitations.
lesson: A useful README explains the problem, data source, setup, approach and findings. Include the exact command needed to reproduce the work.
Separate measured outcomes from hypothetical opportunities. Link your notebook or dashboard and acknowledge dataset limitations.
tasks: Publish a repository with a reproducible README.
Write three findings supported by a table or chart.

questions.prompt: Which collection maps unique keys to values?
questions.explanation: A dictionary stores key-value pairs; each key identifies one value.

questions.prompt: What does a function return if it reaches the end without a return statement?
questions.explanation: Python returns None when no explicit return value is supplied.

questions.prompt: What is the best first step before filling missing values?
questions.explanation: The meaning and pattern of missing data should guide the treatment.

questions.prompt: Which operation summarises revenue by region in pandas?
questions.explanation: Grouping by region and summing revenue creates one aggregate per region.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters aggregated groups?
questions.explanation: HAVING applies conditions to groups after aggregation.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(column_name) count?
questions.explanation: COUNT(column_name) excludes null values. COUNT(*) counts rows.

questions.prompt: Which statistic is generally less sensitive to extreme outliers?
questions.explanation: The median depends on rank rather than the magnitude of extreme values.

questions.prompt: A strong correlation by itself establishes…
questions.explanation: Correlation measures association. A causal claim needs additional evidence.

questions.prompt: Which chart is a natural starting point for monthly revenue trends?
questions.explanation: A line chart displays ordered observations over time.

questions.prompt: How does a window function differ from GROUP BY?
questions.explanation: Window functions calculate over related rows without collapsing each group.

questions.prompt: When should a scaler be fitted?
questions.explanation: Fit preprocessing on training data and apply the learned transformation to other splits.

questions.prompt: For a rare positive class, what should accompany accuracy?
questions.explanation: Precision and recall help expose performance on the rare positive class.

questions.prompt: Feature importance proves a feature causes the outcome.
questions.explanation: Importance describes the model, not a causal intervention.

questions.prompt: What should happen before selecting dashboard charts?
options: Choose as many colours as possible
questions.explanation: Metric definitions and intended decisions determine what the dashboard needs to show.

questions.prompt: A statistically significant effect is always worth implementing.
questions.explanation: Practical value also depends on effect size, uncertainty, risks and implementation costs.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 7 // 2 in Python?
questions.explanation: Floor division returns the integer floor of the quotient.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 7 % 3?
questions.explanation: The remainder after dividing 7 by 3 is 1.

questions.prompt: What does 2 ** 3 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The ** operator performs exponentiation: 2 cubed is 8.

questions.prompt: What does len([4, 4, 9]) return?
questions.explanation: len counts elements, including repeated values.
A negative index of -1 selects the last element.
A slice includes its start position and excludes its stop position.

questions.prompt: What does list(range(2, 7, 2)) produce?
questions.explanation: range advances by 2 from 2 and stops before 7.

questions.prompt: What is bool([])?
questions.explanation: An empty list is false in a Boolean context.

questions.prompt: What is bool('False')?
questions.explanation: Any nonempty string is truthy, regardless of its spelling.

questions.prompt: Which expression checks whether x is None?
questions.explanation: None is a singleton, so identity comparison is the standard check.

questions.prompt: Which built-in collection is immutable?
questions.explanation: A tuple's element references cannot be reassigned after creation.

questions.prompt: Which value can be a dictionary key?
questions.explanation: A tuple containing only hashable values is hashable.

questions.prompt: What does set([1, 1, 2]) contain?
questions.explanation: Sets store distinct elements rather than repeated occurrences.

questions.prompt: What happens when list.append(x) is called?
options: One item is added to the list
Every item in x is necessarily added separately
questions.explanation: append adds its argument as one element.

questions.prompt: Which method adds each item from an iterable to a list?
questions.explanation: extend consumes the iterable and adds its elements individually.

questions.prompt: What does sorted([3, 1, 2]) return?
questions.explanation: sorted creates a new sorted list without modifying the input list.

questions.prompt: For x = [3, 1], what does x.sort() return?
questions.explanation: list.sort mutates the list in place and returns None.

questions.prompt: What is 'data'.upper()?
questions.explanation: upper returns a string with cased characters converted to uppercase.

questions.prompt: What does ' a '.strip() return?
questions.explanation: strip removes leading and trailing whitespace by default.

questions.prompt: What is 'a,b,c'.split(',')?
questions.explanation: split returns a list separated at the specified delimiter.

questions.prompt: What is '-'.join(['a', 'b'])?
questions.explanation: join inserts the separator between the supplied strings.

questions.prompt: What is int('12')?
questions.explanation: int parses a valid integer string into an integer.

questions.prompt: What does int('12.5') do?
questions.explanation: A decimal-point string is not accepted directly by int.

questions.prompt: What does enumerate(['x', 'y']) provide when iterated?
questions.explanation: enumerate supplies a counter alongside each element.

questions.prompt: With equal-length inputs, what does zip(a, b) produce?
questions.explanation: zip aligns the iterables position by position.

questions.prompt: By default, when does zip stop for unequal-length inputs?
options: After filling missing items with zero
questions.explanation: Ordinary zip truncates at the shortest iterable.

questions.prompt: What does break do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: break stops the innermost loop containing it.

questions.prompt: What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Resets the loop counter to zero
questions.explanation: continue skips the remaining statements in the current iteration.

questions.prompt: Which block executes when a matching exception is caught?
questions.explanation: An except clause handles exceptions matching its specified type.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a finally block?
options: Run cleanup when leaving the try statement
Run only when no exception occurs
Replace every return value with None
questions.explanation: finally normally executes whether the try block succeeds or raises an exception.

questions.prompt: Why use with open(path) as f?
options: To load the entire file into memory automatically
To close the file when the block exits
questions.explanation: The file context manager closes the file on normal or exceptional exit.

questions.prompt: Which file mode appends without truncating existing content?
questions.explanation: Append mode writes at the end of an existing file.

questions.prompt: Which file mode truncates an existing file when opened successfully?
questions.explanation: Write mode clears existing contents before writing.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of def f(items=[])?
options: The list is recreated on every call
The default list is shared across calls
questions.explanation: Default arguments are evaluated once when the function is defined.

questions.prompt: Which pattern avoids a shared mutable default?
options: Use None and create a list inside the function
Call append in the default expression
Use an empty dictionary as the default
questions.explanation: A fresh list can be created on each call when the default is None.

questions.prompt: After a = [1]; b = a; b.append(2), what is a?
questions.explanation: Both names refer to the same mutable list.

questions.prompt: For a flat list a, what does a.copy() create?
options: A deep copy of every nested object
A second name for the same list
questions.explanation: A shallow copy duplicates the outer list but shares referenced elements.

questions.prompt: Why can a shallow copy of a nested list still share changes?
options: The outer list is always identical
questions.explanation: Shallow copying preserves references to nested mutable objects.

questions.prompt: What is [x*x for x in [1, 2, 3]]?
questions.explanation: The comprehension evaluates the square of each input.

questions.prompt: What is [x for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0]?
questions.explanation: The condition retains values with an even remainder test, including zero.

questions.prompt: What does a generator usually enable?
questions.explanation: A generator can yield values on demand instead of materialising them all.

questions.prompt: Which keyword produces a value from a generator function?
questions.explanation: yield suspends a generator and makes a value available to its caller.

questions.prompt: What does d.get('missing', 0) return when the key is absent?
questions.explanation: get returns the supplied default when the key is not present.

questions.prompt: What does accessing d['missing'] do when that key is absent?
questions.explanation: Direct dictionary indexing requires the key to exist.

questions.prompt: What does 'x' in {'x': 4} test?
options: Whether the dictionary has four items
questions.explanation: Membership on a dictionary checks its keys.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between == and is?
options: Both always mean the same thing
questions.explanation: == compares values according to the objects; is compares identity.

questions.prompt: What does sum([]) return with its default start?
questions.explanation: sum starts at zero by default and adds no elements for an empty iterable.

questions.prompt: Which approach best tests a revenue function?
options: Check normal, empty and adjustment cases
Check only one large positive input
questions.explanation: Different input classes reveal errors that a single typical example misses.

questions.prompt: What does df.shape report?
questions.explanation: shape is a tuple containing the number of rows and columns.

questions.prompt: Which method previews the first five rows by default?
questions.explanation: head shows the initial rows in their existing order.

questions.prompt: Which property lists column data types?
questions.explanation: dtypes reports the dtype of each column.

questions.prompt: Which method gives column types and non-null counts?
questions.explanation: info provides a concise structural summary including non-null counts.

questions.prompt: Which expression identifies missing values?
questions.explanation: isna returns a Boolean mask for recognised missing values.

questions.prompt: How do you count missing values per column?
questions.explanation: Summing the Boolean missing-value mask counts missing entries in each column.

questions.prompt: How do you calculate missing proportions per column?
questions.explanation: The mean of a Boolean mask is the fraction of True values.

questions.prompt: Which selector is primarily label-based?
options: An ordinary Python slice on a list
questions.explanation: loc selects using index and column labels.

questions.prompt: Which selector is primarily integer-position-based?
questions.explanation: iloc selects by zero-based integer positions.

questions.prompt: What does df.iloc[0] select?
options: All rows with a zero value
The row labelled 0 in every case
questions.explanation: iloc ignores index labels and selects by position.

questions.prompt: What does df[['a', 'b']] return for existing columns?
questions.explanation: A list of column names selects a DataFrame subset.

questions.prompt: How do you retain rows where price exceeds 100?
questions.explanation: A Boolean row mask filters rows satisfying the comparison.

questions.prompt: Which operator combines two pandas Boolean Series elementwise with AND?
questions.explanation: The & operator combines masks elementwise; parenthesise each comparison.

questions.prompt: How should compound pandas comparison masks be grouped?
options: Convert every mask to a string
questions.explanation: Parentheses prevent operator-precedence mistakes in compound masks.

questions.prompt: Which method tests membership in a list of allowed values?
questions.explanation: Series.isin produces a Boolean membership mask.

questions.prompt: Which method removes duplicate rows?
questions.explanation: drop_duplicates removes repeated rows based on the selected columns.

questions.prompt: Which method flags duplicate rows without removing them?
questions.explanation: duplicated returns a Boolean Series marking duplicate occurrences.

questions.prompt: Why inspect duplicate business keys before dropping rows?
options: Repeated keys can represent legitimate events
Every repeated key is an error
questions.explanation: The intended row grain determines whether repeated keys are valid.

questions.prompt: Which operation renames column old to new?
questions.explanation: The columns mapping changes column labels rather than cell values.

questions.prompt: Which method changes the row order by a column's values?
questions.explanation: sort_values orders rows using one or more data columns.

questions.prompt: What does reset_index(drop=True) do?
options: Replaces the index without retaining it as a column
questions.explanation: drop=True discards the old index instead of inserting it into the columns.

questions.prompt: What does set_index('customer_id') normally use as the index?
questions.explanation: set_index promotes the chosen column values to row labels.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps all left-table keys and matching right rows?
questions.explanation: A left join retains left rows even when the right table has no match.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps only keys found in both inputs?
questions.explanation: An inner join returns matched combinations only.

questions.prompt: What can a many-to-many merge do to row counts?
options: Always preserve the left row count
Always reduce to one row per key
questions.explanation: Every left match combines with every right match for a repeated key.

questions.prompt: Which merge argument checks expected key cardinality?
questions.explanation: validate can enforce relationships such as one_to_one or many_to_one.

questions.prompt: What does merge(..., indicator=True) add?
questions.explanation: The indicator identifies left-only, right-only and matched rows.

questions.prompt: Which operation stacks similarly structured DataFrames vertically?
questions.explanation: Concatenation along axis 0 adds rows.

questions.prompt: What should you check before concatenating tables?
questions.explanation: Matching names alone do not guarantee compatible data semantics.

questions.prompt: Which groupby method broadcasts a group statistic back to rows?
questions.explanation: transform returns values aligned to the original group rows.

questions.prompt: Which groupby operation typically reduces groups to summaries?
questions.explanation: Aggregation computes group-level summaries rather than retaining one output per row.

questions.prompt: How does groupby.size differ from groupby.count?
options: size counts columns; count counts rows
Both always ignore null rows entirely
size counts rows; count excludes nulls per column
questions.explanation: size measures group length, whereas count counts non-null entries per column.

questions.prompt: What does value_counts() usually summarise for a Series?
questions.explanation: value_counts counts occurrences of each value, excluding missing values by default.

questions.prompt: Which operation converts date strings to datetime values?
questions.explanation: to_datetime parses values into pandas datetime representations.

questions.prompt: With pd.to_datetime, what does errors='coerce' do to invalid dates?
questions.explanation: Coercion marks unparseable dates as missing datetime values.

questions.prompt: How do you access the year of a datetime Series s?
questions.explanation: The dt accessor exposes datetime components for a datetime Series.

questions.prompt: What should precede monthly resampling of a time-indexed table?
options: Convert the index to random integers
questions.explanation: Time-based resampling requires an appropriate time index or an explicit time column.

questions.prompt: What does a rolling mean help show?
options: The exact causal effect of time
Local trends over a moving window
questions.explanation: A rolling mean smooths short-term fluctuations within successive windows.

questions.prompt: Why specify min_periods for a rolling calculation?
options: To set the number of columns
questions.explanation: min_periods determines how much non-missing data is required for an output.

questions.prompt: What does Series.shift(1) normally do?
options: Aligns each value with the following row position
questions.explanation: A one-period shift is useful for comparing a row with the prior observation.

questions.prompt: Before calculating a customer-level lag, what is essential?
questions.explanation: Lag calculations depend on the order within each customer's observations.

questions.prompt: What does melt typically do?
options: Reshapes wide columns into long rows
questions.explanation: melt unpivots selected columns into variable-value rows.

questions.prompt: Why might pivot fail with duplicate index-column pairs?
options: The table must have exactly two rows
Pivot cannot handle any missing values
Each output cell would have multiple input values
questions.explanation: pivot does not aggregate multiple values for the same output cell.

questions.prompt: Which reshaping function can aggregate duplicate index-column pairs?
questions.explanation: pivot_table supports aggregation when multiple observations share a cell.

questions.prompt: What does pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce') do to invalid numbers?
questions.explanation: Invalid numeric strings become missing values under coercion.

questions.prompt: Which assignment clearly targets selected rows and one column?
questions.explanation: A single loc assignment explicitly targets the original DataFrame.

questions.prompt: Why preserve a raw copy of imported data?
options: To audit and reproduce cleaning decisions
questions.explanation: An untouched source helps trace how transformations changed the data.

questions.prompt: Which validation is useful after currency conversion?
options: Assume every numeric column is currency
Check units and reconcile selected calculations
questions.explanation: Conversion must use the intended units, rates and calculation direction.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause selects rows before grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE evaluates conditions on input rows before aggregation.

questions.prompt: Which SQL keyword removes duplicate result rows?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicates across the selected expressions.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders count?
questions.explanation: Without a filter, COUNT(*) counts every row.

questions.prompt: How should SQL test for a null value?
questions.explanation: NULL represents missing information and requires a null predicate.

questions.prompt: What is the result of NULL = NULL in standard SQL logic?
questions.explanation: Ordinary comparisons involving NULL evaluate to unknown.

questions.prompt: Which rows survive a WHERE predicate?
options: Only rows where it is false
Rows where it is true or unknown
Rows where the predicate is true
questions.explanation: WHERE retains true results and excludes false or unknown results.

questions.prompt: What does COALESCE(a, b, 0) return?
questions.explanation: COALESCE checks arguments in order and returns the first non-null value.

questions.prompt: Why use NULLIF(denominator, 0) in division?
options: To turn all nulls into one
To turn a zero denominator into NULL
questions.explanation: NULLIF prevents division by zero by replacing zero with NULL.

questions.prompt: What does GROUP BY customer_id establish?
options: One aggregate group per customer_id value
One output row per original order always
questions.explanation: GROUP BY partitions rows into groups for aggregation.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate ignores null amounts when calculating an average?
questions.explanation: AVG uses non-null values of its argument.

questions.prompt: For amounts 10, 20 and NULL, what is AVG(amount)?
questions.explanation: AVG excludes NULL, so the calculation is 30 divided by 2.

questions.prompt: For amounts 10, 20 and NULL, what is COUNT(amount)?
questions.explanation: COUNT of a column counts only non-null values.

questions.prompt: What does SUM(amount) return over no input rows in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: SUM returns NULL for no rows; use COALESCE if a zero is appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which clause explicitly orders a result?
questions.explanation: Only an explicit ordering should be relied on for result order.

questions.prompt: How do you request highest revenue first?
questions.explanation: DESC sorts values in descending order.

questions.prompt: Why add a unique tie-breaker to ORDER BY with LIMIT?
questions.explanation: A unique secondary key removes ambiguity among equal sort values.

questions.prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Every left row regardless of matches
questions.explanation: An inner join retains matched combinations from both inputs.

questions.prompt: What does a LEFT JOIN produce for an unmatched left row?
questions.explanation: A left join preserves the row and fills the unmatched right side with NULL.

questions.prompt: What does a CROSS JOIN return?
questions.explanation: A cross join forms the Cartesian product of its inputs.

questions.prompt: Two tables have 3 and 4 rows. How many rows does their CROSS JOIN have?
questions.explanation: Each of the 3 rows combines with each of the 4 rows.

questions.prompt: A key occurs twice on the left and three times on the right. How many matched combinations does that key produce?
questions.explanation: The join pairs each left occurrence with each right occurrence.

questions.prompt: What can a right-table filter in WHERE do after a LEFT JOIN?
options: Remove rows with no right match
Convert the join into a cross join
questions.explanation: An ordinary comparison on right-side NULLs is not true, so unmatched rows can be filtered out.

questions.prompt: Where can a right-side matching condition go to preserve unmatched left rows?
options: In the LEFT JOIN ON clause
questions.explanation: An ON condition controls matches without discarding unmatched left rows.

questions.prompt: Which construct checks whether a subquery returns any rows?
questions.explanation: EXISTS tests the presence of at least one subquery row.

questions.prompt: Why can NOT IN behave unexpectedly if its subquery includes NULL?
options: The query automatically becomes a cross join
NULL is always treated as zero
questions.explanation: A NULL in the candidate set can make a nonmatching comparison unknown.

questions.prompt: Which pattern commonly avoids NOT IN's null trap for anti-matching?
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS checks for actual matching rows rather than membership with unknown values.

questions.prompt: What does UNION do by default?
options: Combines results and removes duplicate rows
Sorts by every numeric column descending
Combines results and keeps all duplicates
questions.explanation: UNION performs set-style combination with duplicate elimination.

questions.prompt: What does UNION ALL preserve?
options: Only rows from the first query
questions.explanation: UNION ALL appends both result sets without deduplication.

questions.prompt: What must corresponding UNION columns have?
questions.explanation: The result sets need compatible column counts and types.

questions.prompt: Which SQL expression supports conditional values?
questions.explanation: CASE selects a result based on conditions.

questions.prompt: What does CASE return if no condition matches and ELSE is omitted?
questions.explanation: A CASE expression without a matching branch defaults to NULL.

questions.prompt: What does a common table expression mainly provide?
options: A named query result within a statement
questions.explanation: A CTE gives a subquery a name for use in the containing statement.

questions.prompt: Which keyword introduces a CTE?
questions.explanation: WITH introduces one or more common table expressions.

questions.prompt: What does a primary key enforce?
options: Automatic removal of duplicates from every query
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot contain NULL.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key enforce?
options: An automatic inner join in every query
A reference to permitted keys in another or the same table
questions.explanation: A foreign key constrains references according to the declared relationship.

questions.prompt: What is database normalisation intended to reduce?
questions.explanation: Normalisation structures related facts to reduce inconsistent repeated storage.

questions.prompt: When can an index help a query?
options: Only for SELECT * with no filters
Only when the table has no rows
When it supports selective filtering or useful ordering
Whenever any query exists, without trade-offs
questions.explanation: An appropriate index can reduce the data examined or sorting work.

questions.prompt: What is a common cost of adding indexes?
questions.explanation: Inserts and updates may need to maintain additional index structures.

questions.prompt: What does EXPLAIN show in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN describes how the planner intends to execute the statement.

questions.prompt: Why treat EXPLAIN ANALYZE on modifying statements carefully?
options: It reads only a cached plan
questions.explanation: ANALYZE executes the statement to collect actual runtime measurements.

questions.prompt: What does COMMIT do?
options: Makes the current transaction's changes permanent
questions.explanation: COMMIT completes a transaction and persists its successful changes.

questions.prompt: What does ROLLBACK do before commit?
options: Undoes changes in the current transaction
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK abandons the uncommitted transaction.

questions.prompt: What is an SQL injection defence for user-supplied values?
options: Hiding the query in the frontend
questions.explanation: Parameters keep supplied values separate from executable SQL structure.

questions.prompt: Why avoid SELECT * in a stable reporting interface?
options: Unexpected schema changes can alter the output
It automatically creates duplicate columns in all queries
questions.explanation: Explicit columns make the report contract clearer and more stable.

questions.prompt: What does CAST(amount AS numeric) request?
options: A conversion to the numeric type
questions.explanation: CAST explicitly converts an expression to the specified type when valid.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does LIKE 'A%' match?
options: Every string containing a lowercase a only
questions.explanation: The percent wildcard matches any sequence after the initial A.

questions.prompt: In SQL LIKE patterns, what does underscore represent?
questions.explanation: The underscore wildcard matches exactly one character.

questions.prompt: Why use a half-open timestamp interval such as >= start AND < next_day?
options: It converts timestamps into dates automatically
It handles all times before the next boundary
It guarantees the same local timezone
questions.explanation: An exclusive next boundary avoids guessing the final representable instant of a day.

questions.prompt: What should be clarified before grouping timestamps into days?
options: The timezone defining the reporting day
questions.explanation: A timestamp can belong to different calendar days in different timezones.

questions.prompt: Which value should be summed for line-item revenue before tax?
options: Customer ID multiplied by order ID
The count of product names only
questions.explanation: Revenue at the line grain is quantity times the applicable price, with adjustments defined separately.

questions.prompt: Why can joining order totals to order lines overstate revenue?
options: The currency changes during the join
Inner joins duplicate every unique key
The order total repeats for each line
questions.explanation: An order-level amount should not be summed repeatedly at a finer line-item grain.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) count?
questions.explanation: COUNT DISTINCT counts unique non-null values of the expression.

questions.prompt: When is a view useful?
options: To make all tables writable by everyone
To expose a reusable query definition
To guarantee every query is faster
questions.explanation: A normal view stores a query definition rather than automatically storing its result.

questions.prompt: For values 2, 4 and 6, what is the arithmetic mean?
questions.explanation: Their sum is 12 and there are 3 values.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 3, 9, 10 and 20?
questions.explanation: The middle value of the sorted five-element sample is 9.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 8 and 10?
questions.explanation: For an even count, average the two middle values: (4 + 8) / 2.

questions.prompt: What is the mode of 1, 2, 2, 3, 5?
questions.explanation: The mode is the most frequent value.

questions.prompt: What does standard deviation describe?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures dispersion in the original measurement units.

questions.prompt: How do variance units relate to the original variable?
questions.explanation: Variance averages squared deviations and therefore has squared units.

questions.prompt: What is the interquartile range?
questions.explanation: The IQR measures the width of the middle half of the distribution.

questions.prompt: What does a right-skewed distribution have?
options: A longer tail toward smaller values
A longer tail toward larger values
questions.explanation: Right skew refers to an extended upper-value tail.

questions.prompt: Why report both mean and median income?
options: They reveal how skew can affect the centre
questions.explanation: The mean can be pulled upward by high incomes while the median reflects the middle rank.

questions.prompt: What is a population in a statistical study?
questions.explanation: The population is the set about which the study aims to draw conclusions.

questions.prompt: What is a sample statistic?
options: A quantity calculated from observed sample data
An unknown fixed population quantity only
questions.explanation: Statistics summarise samples; parameters describe populations.

questions.prompt: What is selection bias?
options: Systematic distortion from how observations enter a sample
A property of all large samples
questions.explanation: A selected sample can differ systematically from the target population.

questions.prompt: Why can a voluntary online poll be unrepresentative?
options: Online answers must always be false
A large sample eliminates every bias
Participation may depend on interest or access
The poll has too many columns
questions.explanation: Self-selection and unequal access can change who participates.

questions.prompt: What is survivorship bias?
options: Studying only cases that remain observable
Giving every case equal selection probability
questions.explanation: Ignoring failures or disappearances can distort conclusions about the original group.

questions.prompt: What is a confounder?
options: The measured outcome itself in every study
A variable related to both exposure and outcome
questions.explanation: A common influence can create or distort an observed exposure-outcome association.

questions.prompt: What does random sampling mainly support?
questions.explanation: Probability sampling helps relate a sample to its population.

questions.prompt: What does random assignment mainly support?
options: Making a sample representative of all people
Comparing treatment effects with less confounding
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances causes of outcomes in expectation across treatment groups.

questions.prompt: What is an independent event relationship?
options: Knowing one event does not change the other's probability
The two events cannot occur together
questions.explanation: Independence means the joint probability factors into the product of marginal probabilities.

questions.prompt: For independent events with probabilities 0.4 and 0.5, what is their joint probability?
questions.explanation: Multiply independent probabilities: 0.4 times 0.5 equals 0.2.

questions.prompt: What is P(not A) when P(A) = 0.3?
questions.explanation: An event and its complement have probabilities summing to 1.

questions.prompt: What is P(A given B)?
options: The probability of A plus B
The probability of B given A in every case
The probability of A among outcomes satisfying B
The probability that neither event occurs
questions.explanation: Conditioning restricts the reference set to cases where B occurs.

questions.prompt: Why are P(A given B) and P(B given A) not generally equal?
options: Conditional probabilities must sum to one
questions.explanation: The denominators differ, so reversing the condition changes the probability.

questions.prompt: What is a Bernoulli variable?
options: A variable with two outcomes encoded 0 and 1
A count with no upper bound
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli variable represents one binary trial.

questions.prompt: Which model counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with common success probability?
questions.explanation: The binomial model uses a fixed number of comparable independent Bernoulli trials.

questions.prompt: Which distribution commonly models counts in a fixed interval under a constant independent event rate?
questions.explanation: The Poisson model describes event counts under its rate and independence assumptions.

questions.prompt: What is the expected number of successes in 10 independent trials with success probability 0.2?
questions.explanation: The binomial expectation is n times p: 10 times 0.2.

questions.prompt: For a normal distribution, where are the mean and median?
questions.explanation: A normal distribution is symmetric around its mean.

questions.prompt: What is a z-score?
options: A raw percentile expressed as currency
A deviation from the mean measured in standard deviations
questions.explanation: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.

questions.prompt: If x = 70, mean = 50 and standard deviation = 10, what is the z-score?
questions.explanation: The standardised deviation is (70 - 50) / 10 = 2.

questions.prompt: What does the central limit theorem concern under suitable conditions?
options: The sampling distribution of a mean
Every raw dataset becoming normally distributed
questions.explanation: Means from repeated sufficiently large samples can be approximately normal even when raw data are not.

questions.prompt: What is a standard error?
options: The variation among all individual measurements only
The sampling variability of an estimator
questions.explanation: A standard error describes how an estimate varies across repeated samples.

questions.prompt: Under independent sampling with fixed variance, what happens to the mean's standard error when sample size quadruples?
questions.explanation: The standard error scales with the inverse square root of sample size.

questions.prompt: What does a frequentist 95% confidence procedure mean?
options: Each observed value has a 95% chance of being correct
95% of the population must lie in each interval
Its intervals cover the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples
questions.explanation: Coverage describes the long-run behaviour of the interval construction procedure.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to a confidence interval when the confidence level increases, all else equal?
options: It contains fewer plausible parameter values
questions.explanation: Higher coverage requires a wider interval with the same data and method.

questions.prompt: What is a null hypothesis?
options: A conclusion that data are missing
A specified claim assessed by a test
A guarantee that no effect exists
questions.explanation: A test evaluates data relative to a stated null model or claim.

questions.prompt: What is a p-value?
options: The size of the observed effect
The probability, under the null model, of a result at least as extreme as observed
The probability that the null is true
The probability the data were fabricated
questions.explanation: A p-value is conditional on the null assumptions, not a posterior probability of the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: What is a Type I error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive in hypothesis testing.

questions.prompt: What is a Type II error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative in hypothesis testing.

questions.prompt: What is statistical power?
options: The confidence level of every chart
The probability of rejecting a false null for a specified alternative
The number of decimal places reported
The probability that every estimate is exact
questions.explanation: Power depends on effect size, variability, sample size and the testing procedure.

questions.prompt: Why report an effect size alongside a p-value?
options: To describe the magnitude of the difference
questions.explanation: A small p-value does not indicate whether an effect is large or useful.

questions.prompt: What does failing to reject a null establish?
options: Insufficient evidence against it under the test
Proof that the null is true
Proof that the effect is exactly zero
questions.explanation: Non-rejection can reflect limited information or low power.

questions.prompt: Why adjust when testing many hypotheses?
options: To control a chosen multiple-testing error rate
To guarantee every discovery is true
To remove the need for a hypothesis
questions.explanation: Many tests create more opportunities for false positives.

questions.prompt: What does a bootstrap typically resample?
options: The population without using the sample
Only the fitted coefficients without data
questions.explanation: Bootstrap resampling approximates sampling variability using the observed sample.

questions.prompt: Why might an ordinary row bootstrap be inappropriate for a time series?
options: Rows may be dependent over time
A time series has no sampling variation
questions.explanation: Resampling individual dependent rows can destroy the dependence structure.

questions.prompt: Which correlation targets monotonic association using ranks?
options: A raw covariance in all cases
questions.explanation: Spearman correlation measures association between ranked values.

questions.prompt: What does Pearson correlation primarily measure?
questions.explanation: Pearson correlation can be small even when a strong nonlinear relationship exists.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of a correlation computed on pooled groups?
options: It automatically adjusts for group membership
It can differ from within-group relationships
It always equals every subgroup correlation
questions.explanation: Mixing groups can create or reverse an aggregate association.

questions.prompt: What is an outlier investigation's best first step?
options: Replace every extreme value with the mean
questions.explanation: Extreme values may be errors or valid observations with important context.

questions.prompt: Why does measurement reliability matter?
options: Repeated measurements must always match exactly
Noise can weaken or distort observed relationships
questions.explanation: Measurement error can affect estimates even when the sampling design is sound.

questions.prompt: For groups of sizes 10 and 30 with means 20 and 40, what is the combined mean?
questions.explanation: The weighted mean is (10 times 20 + 30 times 40) / 40 = 35.

questions.prompt: Why can averaging percentages across unequal groups mislead?
options: All percentages share the same denominator
questions.explanation: A pooled rate must weight each group by its relevant denominator.

questions.prompt: What does an empirical percentile describe?
options: A value's position relative to observed data
The probability that the dataset is correct
A causal effect of increasing a value
questions.explanation: Percentiles summarise relative location in a distribution.

questions.prompt: What is a prediction interval intended to cover?
options: A future observation under the model
questions.explanation: Prediction intervals include uncertainty about an individual future outcome.

questions.prompt: Which chart best compares revenue across five product categories?
questions.explanation: Bars provide a common baseline for comparing categorical magnitudes.

questions.prompt: Which chart shows the distribution of a continuous variable using bins?
questions.explanation: A histogram groups numeric values into intervals and shows their frequencies.

questions.prompt: What is a scatter plot useful for?
options: Inspecting relationships between two numeric variables
questions.explanation: Each point locates an observation along two numeric axes.

questions.prompt: Why can histogram bin width change the visual story?
options: It changes how observations are grouped
It changes the original data values
questions.explanation: Different bin widths can reveal or conceal distributional features.

questions.prompt: When is a box plot useful?
options: Comparing medians and spread across groups
Proving the mean equals the median
questions.explanation: Box plots summarise quartiles and can flag potential outliers.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of a truncated bar-chart baseline?
questions.explanation: Bar lengths encode magnitude, so removing the zero baseline can distort comparisons.

questions.prompt: When can a nonzero line-chart baseline be reasonable?
options: Only when the data are fabricated
When clearly labelled and needed to inspect variation
When it proves the trend is causal
questions.explanation: Line charts encode position and change; a clearly indicated range can highlight variation.

questions.prompt: What does a logarithmic axis represent through equal distances?
questions.explanation: Equal steps on a log axis correspond to multiplying by a constant factor.

questions.prompt: Why can't zero be shown on an ordinary logarithmic axis?
options: The logarithm of zero is undefined
questions.explanation: The ordinary logarithm is defined only for positive real values.

questions.prompt: Which palette suits ordered low-to-high values?
questions.explanation: A sequential palette changes systematically with magnitude.

questions.prompt: Which palette suits deviations around a meaningful midpoint?
options: A separate hue for every observation
questions.explanation: Diverging scales distinguish values above and below a reference point.

questions.prompt: Which palette suits distinct categories without order?
questions.explanation: Qualitative colours distinguish categories without implying magnitude.

questions.prompt: Why avoid relying on red versus green alone?
options: Red and green are always invisible
Some viewers cannot reliably distinguish them
questions.explanation: Labels, shapes or other cues make distinctions more accessible.

questions.prompt: What should an axis label usually include?
questions.explanation: Units make the numerical scale interpretable.

questions.prompt: What is a useful chart title?
options: A clear question or supported finding
questions.explanation: A specific title helps readers understand the chart's purpose.

questions.prompt: When comparing several small charts, what improves fair comparison?
options: A different hidden scale for each chart
questions.explanation: Shared scales allow visual magnitudes to be compared directly.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of dual-axis charts?
options: Arbitrary scales can suggest a misleading relationship
questions.explanation: Independent axis choices can make unrelated series appear aligned.

questions.prompt: What is overplotting?
options: Many marks overlap and hide data density
Too many decimal places in a table
A dataset with no duplicate rows
questions.explanation: Overlapping points can conceal concentrations and variation.

questions.prompt: Which technique can reduce scatter-plot overplotting?
options: Making every point fully opaque and larger
questions.explanation: Transparency and aggregation reveal dense regions more clearly.

questions.prompt: Why can a pie chart with many categories be hard to read?
options: Similar angles are difficult to compare
It always has a time axis
questions.explanation: Many small sectors make precise comparisons difficult.

questions.prompt: When is a 100% stacked bar chart useful?
questions.explanation: Each bar is normalised to 100%, emphasising shares rather than totals.

questions.prompt: What information is lost in a 100% stacked bar chart without total labels?
questions.explanation: Equal bar lengths hide variation in group size.

questions.prompt: What can a heatmap encode with colour?
questions.explanation: Heatmaps map table-cell values to a colour scale.

questions.prompt: Why annotate a correlation heatmap's scale?
options: To prove all correlations are causal
questions.explanation: A clear legend explains how colours correspond to correlation values.

questions.prompt: What should an uncertainty band around a line specify?
questions.explanation: Confidence, prediction and other intervals convey different kinds of uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Why should a chart disclose a small subgroup sample size?
options: Small groups always have zero variance
questions.explanation: Readers need group sizes to assess the reliability of a comparison.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate way to show missing months in a time series?
options: Connect observations and claim continuous measurement
Replace every gap with the next peak
Indicate the gap rather than silently inventing values
questions.explanation: Visible gaps distinguish unobserved periods from measured values.

questions.prompt: When is a map more useful than a bar chart?
options: When geographic location is central to the question
When exact ranking is the only task
questions.explanation: Maps are most helpful when spatial patterns matter.

questions.prompt: Why can total counts on a population map mislead?
options: Every region has the same population
Large populations can dominate the pattern
questions.explanation: Rates or appropriate denominators may be needed for fair geographic comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which display is best when readers need exact values?
questions.explanation: Tables support precise lookup better than approximate visual encoding.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of using area to encode magnitude?
options: Readers may compare diameter instead of area
questions.explanation: Bubble sizing must scale area correctly and may still be harder to compare than position.

questions.prompt: Why export vector graphics for suitable charts?
options: They force every chart to be interactive
questions.explanation: Vector marks can scale without the pixelation of a fixed-resolution raster.

questions.prompt: Which takeaway is justified by an observational sales trend?
options: The next campaign will produce identical growth
The campaign definitely caused all growth
Sales rose during the campaign period
questions.explanation: A temporal association alone does not establish a causal effect.

questions.prompt: What does PARTITION BY define in a window function?
options: A final result sort in every case
questions.explanation: Window partitions determine which related rows participate in each calculation.

questions.prompt: What does ORDER BY inside OVER control?
options: Only the final displayed row order
The calculation order within a window
questions.explanation: Window ordering affects functions such as ranks and cumulative sums.

questions.prompt: Does ORDER BY inside OVER guarantee final result order?
options: Only when a table has a primary key
No; use a final ORDER BY
questions.explanation: Window calculation order and output presentation order are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: Which function assigns consecutive row numbers within a partition?
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequence to rows within each partition.

questions.prompt: Why add a unique tie-breaker when using ROW_NUMBER?
options: To convert the result to text
To make equal values receive equal row numbers
To choose a repeatable order among ties
questions.explanation: Tied ordering keys leave the row-number assignment ambiguous without another key.

questions.prompt: What ranks does RANK assign to values 100, 100, 90 in descending order?
questions.explanation: RANK leaves gaps after ties according to the number of preceding rows.

questions.prompt: What ranks does DENSE_RANK assign to values 100, 100, 90 descending?
questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK advances to the next rank without gaps after ties.

questions.prompt: Which function retrieves a preceding row's value?
questions.explanation: LAG accesses an earlier row according to the window ordering.

questions.prompt: Which function retrieves a following row's value?
questions.explanation: LEAD accesses a later row according to the window ordering.

questions.prompt: What does LAG(value) return for the first row when no default is supplied?
questions.explanation: There is no preceding row, so the default result is NULL.

questions.prompt: What does LAG(value, 2) access?
questions.explanation: The second argument is an offset in rows within the ordered partition.

questions.prompt: Why is a one-row lag not necessarily yesterday's value?
options: A row must represent a year
Dates may be missing or repeated
questions.explanation: Row offsets follow observations, not necessarily equal calendar intervals.

questions.prompt: Which frame defines a running sum from the first row through the current row?
options: ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
questions.explanation: The frame grows from the partition's start to each current row.

questions.prompt: Which frame defines a three-row trailing average when enough rows exist?
options: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 2 FOLLOWING
questions.explanation: Two preceding rows plus the current row make a trailing window of three rows.

questions.prompt: How many rows are in ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW away from the boundary?
questions.explanation: The frame includes three earlier rows and the current row.

questions.prompt: What does UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING indicate?
questions.explanation: An unbounded following boundary extends to the final row of the current partition.

questions.prompt: What is a key difference between ROWS and RANGE frames?
options: ROWS uses row positions; RANGE uses ordering values and peers
ROWS groups tables; RANGE groups databases
questions.explanation: RANGE frames can include peer rows sharing the current ordering value.

questions.prompt: Why can a default ordered RANGE frame make a running sum jump at ties?
options: It multiplies every value by the rank
It resets the partition on every tie
It includes all peers with the same ordering value
questions.explanation: Peer rows can enter the frame together rather than one at a time.

questions.prompt: How do you compute each row's share of its region's total?
options: amount / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region), with suitable numeric types
SUM(amount) GROUP BY every amount only
questions.explanation: A partitioned sum provides the denominator while retaining each row.

questions.prompt: Why use suitable numeric types when calculating shares in SQL?
options: To force all shares to one
questions.explanation: Integer arithmetic can discard the fractional part in some SQL expressions.

questions.prompt: How can you show a department total next to every employee?
options: GROUP BY employee and return no salary
questions.explanation: A window aggregate retains employee rows while computing a department total.

questions.prompt: How can PostgreSQL filter rows by a computed window rank?
options: Use the rank alias directly in the same WHERE
Calculate it in a subquery or CTE, then filter outside
questions.explanation: Window functions are computed after WHERE, so an outer query can filter the result.

questions.prompt: How do you keep all tied highest values per group?
options: Filter ROW_NUMBER() = 1 and expect all ties
Filter RANK() = 1 with descending value order
questions.explanation: RANK assigns 1 to every tied highest value within a partition.

questions.prompt: How do you choose exactly one latest record per customer deterministically?
options: DENSE_RANK on timestamp with no tie-breaker and keep all rank 1 rows
ROW_NUMBER ordered by timestamp descending and a unique tie-breaker
questions.explanation: A fully ordered row number selects exactly one row per customer.

questions.prompt: What is a danger of LAST_VALUE with a frame ending at CURRENT ROW?
options: It always returns the first table row
It may return the current frame's last value rather than the partition's final value
It cannot be used with text
questions.explanation: LAST_VALUE respects the frame, which may not include the partition's final row.

questions.prompt: Which frame allows LAST_VALUE to inspect the full partition?
options: ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
questions.explanation: An explicit full-partition frame includes the final partition row.

questions.prompt: What does FIRST_VALUE return?
options: The smallest value regardless of ordering
The first value in the current window frame
questions.explanation: FIRST_VALUE follows the window's ordering and frame boundaries.

questions.prompt: What does NTILE(4) aim to create?
options: Four groups with equal value ranges
questions.explanation: NTILE distributes ordered rows across buckets with sizes as equal as possible.

questions.prompt: Can NTILE split equal values into different buckets?
options: No, equal values always stay together
questions.explanation: NTILE assigns buckets by row position, not by keeping tied values together.

questions.prompt: For distinct ascending values, what does CUME_DIST describe?
options: The maximum value divided by the minimum
The fraction of partition rows at or below the current value
The raw difference from the previous value
questions.explanation: CUME_DIST measures the cumulative share including the current row and its peers.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives a partition's row count on every row?
options: COUNT(*) without OVER and without GROUP BY
questions.explanation: A window count repeats the partition size while preserving its rows.

questions.prompt: What does SUM(x) OVER () compute on every result row?
options: The sum over the entire window input
questions.explanation: An empty OVER clause treats all input rows as one partition.

questions.prompt: Why aggregate transactions to daily totals before a daily running total?
options: To define one row per day at the intended grain
To remove every zero day automatically
questions.explanation: The input grain determines what each cumulative step represents.

questions.prompt: Which value is needed for month-over-month percentage change?
questions.explanation: Relative change uses the previous period as the denominator.

questions.prompt: How should percentage change handle a previous value of zero?
options: Use an explicitly defined undefined or special-case policy
questions.explanation: A relative change from zero is not defined by the ordinary ratio formula.

questions.prompt: Why should a cumulative calculation partition by account?
options: To guarantee every account has the same balance
To sort account names by length
To prevent balances from mixing across accounts
questions.explanation: Each account needs its own independent cumulative sequence.

questions.prompt: What does ORDER BY timestamp alone fail to specify when timestamps tie?
options: The account partition key in every case
The numeric type of the amount
questions.explanation: A tie-breaker is needed when an exact event sequence matters.

questions.prompt: Which task benefits from a window function rather than collapsing GROUP BY?
options: Comparing each order to its customer's average
Returning only one total for the entire table
questions.explanation: Window functions preserve each order while adding a customer-level comparison.

questions.prompt: What should define a dashboard's first design decision?
options: The number of available chart types
The decision and audience it supports
questions.explanation: The audience's decision determines which metrics and interactions are useful.

questions.prompt: What is a KPI?
options: A measure tied to an important objective
questions.explanation: A KPI connects a measurable quantity to a business goal.

questions.prompt: Why document a KPI's numerator and denominator?
options: To eliminate the need for filters
questions.explanation: Explicit definitions prevent different users from calculating different metrics with the same name.

questions.prompt: What is average order value when revenue is 1200 across 30 orders?
questions.explanation: Average order value is revenue divided by the number of orders.

questions.prompt: What should a dashboard's date filter make clear?
options: Which date field and period it filters
questions.explanation: Order date, shipment date and payment date can produce different reporting populations.

questions.prompt: What is a star schema?
options: A table with one column only
A model with every possible bidirectional relationship
A fact table connected to descriptive dimension tables
questions.explanation: A star schema separates measurable events from descriptive attributes.

questions.prompt: What normally belongs in a fact table?
options: Events or measurements at a declared grain
questions.explanation: Facts record business observations such as sales line items or daily balances.

questions.prompt: What normally belongs in a dimension table?
options: Descriptive attributes such as product category
questions.explanation: Dimensions provide descriptive context for grouping and filtering facts.

questions.prompt: Why declare the fact table's grain?
options: To clarify what each row represents
To force one row per year
questions.explanation: The grain controls valid joins, aggregations and interpretation.

questions.prompt: What usually characterises the one side of a one-to-many relationship?
questions.explanation: A unique dimension key can relate to many matching fact rows.

questions.prompt: What can ambiguous relationship paths cause?
questions.explanation: Multiple propagation paths can make filter effects difficult to reason about.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a date table?
options: Making missing dates impossible in source data
Consistent calendar attributes for time analysis
questions.explanation: A date dimension supports consistent grouping and time-based comparisons.

questions.prompt: In Power BI, what does a measure generally evaluate under?
options: Only the first row in the source file
A fixed value independent of all filters
questions.explanation: Measures respond to the filters and groupings in a visual.

questions.prompt: How does a calculated column typically differ from a measure in Import mode?
options: It always recalculates for each slicer selection like a measure
It exists only as a chart label
Its row values are computed at refresh and stored
questions.explanation: Calculated columns store row-level results, while measures evaluate for query context.

questions.prompt: What does CALCULATE primarily do in DAX?
options: Evaluate an expression in modified filter context
questions.explanation: CALCULATE changes the filter context used to evaluate an expression.

questions.prompt: Why use DAX DIVIDE for a ratio?
options: It handles a zero or blank denominator with a defined alternative
questions.explanation: DIVIDE provides controlled behaviour for problematic denominators.

questions.prompt: What does SUMX do?
options: Iterates rows and sums an expression
questions.explanation: SUMX evaluates its expression per row of a table and adds the results.

questions.prompt: Why might SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[Price]) be appropriate?
options: Price and quantity must first be summed independently
Revenue requires multiplication at the row grain before summing
questions.explanation: Line-level products must be calculated before aggregation.

questions.prompt: Why can SUM(Qty) * SUM(Price) misstate revenue?
options: It combines totals rather than matching each row's price and quantity
It uses only the latest row
questions.explanation: Multiplying independent column sums introduces cross-products that are not line revenues.

questions.prompt: What does DISTINCTCOUNT measure?
options: The number of distinct values in a column
questions.explanation: Distinct counts are useful for entities such as customers or orders.

questions.prompt: Why might distinct customer counts not add across regions?
options: The total always contains an error
Distinct counts are ordinary additive sums
A customer may appear in multiple regions
questions.explanation: An entity counted in multiple groups should appear once in the overall distinct count.

questions.prompt: What does a slicer provide?
questions.explanation: Slicers let readers control a selected part of filter context.

questions.prompt: What should be tested after adding a slicer?
options: Whether it increases the page count
Its effect on all intended visuals and totals
questions.explanation: Visual interactions and filter propagation may not match expectations.

questions.prompt: What does drill-through help users do?
options: Open a detail page filtered to a selected context
questions.explanation: Drill-through carries a selected context to a more detailed report page.

questions.prompt: What is a useful tooltip?
options: A repeat of every dashboard page
Additional context relevant to the hovered mark
questions.explanation: Tooltips can add detail without overloading the main visual.

questions.prompt: What should a last-refreshed timestamp communicate?
options: The date of the latest Power BI release
The freshness of the displayed data
The date the company was founded
questions.explanation: Readers need to know how current the underlying data are.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish zero from missing in a report?
options: Missing values must always become zero
Both always mean the same thing
No activity and unknown activity are different
Zero values should always be removed
questions.explanation: Conflating absence of events with absence of information can mislead readers.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a filter yields no rows?
options: Report a guaranteed zero for every unknown measure
questions.explanation: An explicit empty state makes the lack of matching data clear.

questions.prompt: What is row-level security intended to restrict?
options: Which rows a user is permitted to access
The colour of a table header
questions.explanation: Row-level security filters data access according to user permissions.

questions.prompt: Why is hiding a report page not sufficient data security?
options: Users cannot query hidden datasets under any circumstances
Hidden content may remain accessible through other routes
questions.explanation: Presentation choices do not replace access-control enforcement.

questions.prompt: What is a useful dashboard performance improvement?
options: Enable all relationships in both directions indiscriminately
Reduce unnecessary visuals and expensive calculations
Add every source column to every page
questions.explanation: Fewer costly queries and simpler visuals can reduce rendering work.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a dashboard reconciliation check?
options: Compare metrics with an independent trusted calculation
questions.explanation: Independent checks catch errors in joins, filters and formulas.

questions.prompt: What should a metric tooltip explain when returns are included?
options: How returns affect the revenue definition
questions.explanation: Refund and return treatment changes the meaning of reported revenue.

questions.prompt: Why provide a data dictionary?
options: To document fields, units and meanings
To increase the number of measures
To guarantee all data are unbiased
To replace every source table with prose
questions.explanation: A dictionary helps maintainers and readers interpret the model consistently.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is most meaningful for a monthly KPI?
options: A period selected after seeing the desired result
A comparable period using a consistent definition
Only the page's maximum font size
An arbitrary number from another metric
questions.explanation: Comparability requires matching definitions and relevant time windows.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of showing only percentage growth?
options: A tiny baseline may make growth look dramatic
questions.explanation: Absolute values and the baseline provide context for a relative change.

questions.prompt: What should an executive overview prioritise?
options: All raw rows on the first page
A small set of decision-relevant measures
questions.explanation: An overview should make the most important decisions and signals easy to find.

questions.prompt: What is a good acceptance check before sharing a dashboard?
options: Test totals, filters, readability and permissions
Check only whether it opens on the creator's computer
questions.explanation: A useful dashboard must be accurate, usable and appropriately accessible.

questions.prompt: What should be specified before starting an A/B test?
questions.explanation: Predefined criteria reduce the temptation to choose favourable outcomes after observing results.

questions.prompt: What is a treatment group?
options: The group assigned the intervention being tested
Only participants who completed every task
The group with the largest sample by definition
questions.explanation: Treatment status is defined by assigned intervention, not by subsequent outcomes.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a control group?
options: Choose the most engaged users only
Provide a comparison for what would happen without the tested change
Remove all costs from the experiment
questions.explanation: A control condition helps estimate the intervention's effect relative to a baseline.

questions.prompt: Why randomise assignment in an experiment?
options: To balance potential confounders in expectation
questions.explanation: Randomisation reduces systematic differences in treatment assignment.

questions.prompt: Why keep a user in the same variant across visits?
options: To ensure every visit has a different design
To avoid contamination from switching experiences
To increase the number of accounts artificially
questions.explanation: Stable assignment supports a consistent user-level treatment.

questions.prompt: What is the experimental unit?
options: The entity independently assigned to treatment
Only the first person who converts
questions.explanation: Assignment may occur at user, store, household or another defined unit.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish experimental units from observation rows?
options: Every row must represent a new randomised user
Repeated rows from one unit are not independent assignments
The distinction only changes chart colours
questions.explanation: Treating repeated observations as independent can understate uncertainty.

questions.prompt: When might store-level randomisation be preferable to customer-level randomisation?
options: When the intervention affects an entire store
When only customer names are measured
When customers never share a store
When every treatment can be isolated by click
questions.explanation: Cluster assignment can match how treatment is delivered and reduce spillovers.

questions.prompt: What is interference between experimental units?
options: One unit's treatment affects another unit's outcome
questions.explanation: Interference violates the assumption that a unit's outcome depends only on its own assignment.

questions.prompt: What is a guardrail metric?
options: A measure used to detect unacceptable side effects
The single metric selected after results are known
questions.explanation: Guardrails help prevent optimising one outcome at unacceptable cost to another.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible guardrail for a checkout conversion test?
options: The number of letters in the variant name
questions.explanation: Payment failures are a relevant potential harm when modifying checkout.

questions.prompt: What is an A/A test?
options: A comparison selected only after launch
A comparison of two different products always
questions.explanation: An A/A test can help assess instrumentation and randomisation behaviour.

questions.prompt: What can a sample-ratio mismatch indicate?
options: A requirement to ignore the experiment
questions.explanation: Unexpected allocation counts warrant investigation before interpreting effects.

questions.prompt: Why assess experiment duration beyond reaching a raw sample count?
options: Day-of-week patterns and business cycles may matter
Longer duration always removes every bias
A test must always last exactly one day
questions.explanation: Representative exposure over relevant cycles can affect interpretation.

questions.prompt: What is a novelty effect?
options: A permanent causal effect by definition
An error caused only by duplicate rows
An initial response to a new experience that may fade
questions.explanation: Early reactions may differ from longer-term behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why can stopping at the first conventional p-value below 0.05 be problematic?
options: It guarantees a large practical effect
It always lowers the false-positive rate
Repeated unadjusted looks can inflate false positives
questions.explanation: Repeated testing needs a procedure that accounts for the stopping rule.

questions.prompt: What is a suitable approach when interim monitoring is required?
options: Restart the p-value calculation until it is small
questions.explanation: A valid sequential design accounts for planned interim decisions.

questions.prompt: What does intention-to-treat analysis compare?
options: Groups according to their original random assignment
Only users who followed instructions perfectly
questions.explanation: Intention-to-treat preserves the assignment-based comparison.

questions.prompt: Why can analysing only treatment completers introduce bias?
options: It makes the control group unnecessary
It preserves every benefit of randomisation automatically
Completion may relate to outcomes and treatment response
questions.explanation: Post-assignment selection can create differences between analysed groups.

questions.prompt: What is attrition in an experiment?
options: Loss of participants or outcome observations
questions.explanation: Missing follow-up outcomes can threaten comparability if losses differ by group.

questions.prompt: What should be checked when attrition differs between variants?
options: Only the colour of the winning button
Whether missingness could bias the effect estimate
Whether the p-value can be rounded down
Whether the smaller group can be ignored
questions.explanation: Differential loss may change which users remain in the analysis.

questions.prompt: What does a minimum detectable effect help plan?
options: Sample size for a target sensitivity
The exact effect that must occur
questions.explanation: An MDE specifies a target effect size that the planned design aims to detect with given power.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to required sample size when the target detectable effect gets smaller?
questions.explanation: Smaller effects are harder to distinguish from random variation.

questions.prompt: What is absolute lift when conversion rises from 10% to 12%?
questions.explanation: Subtract the rates: 12% minus 10% equals 2 percentage points.

questions.prompt: What is relative lift when conversion rises from 10% to 12%?
questions.explanation: The increase of 2 percentage points divided by the 10% baseline is 20%.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish percentage points from percent change?
options: They always mean the same value
questions.explanation: An absolute rate difference is different from a difference relative to the baseline.

questions.prompt: What can a confidence interval spanning zero for a mean difference suggest?
options: A guarantee the test was randomised correctly
Proof that the effect is exactly zero
The data remain compatible with effects on either side of zero
questions.explanation: The interval communicates uncertainty about the direction and magnitude of the effect.

questions.prompt: What is needed to claim practical equivalence?
options: An appropriate equivalence analysis with prespecified margins
