questions.explanation: Failure to detect a difference does not establish that meaningful differences are absent.

questions.prompt: Why prespecify subgroup analyses?
options: To remove the need for sample sizes
To make all subgroup effects equal
To guarantee every subgroup is significant
To limit selective discovery and clarify interpretation
questions.explanation: Exploratory subgroup searches can produce chance findings.

questions.prompt: A treatment helps one subgroup and harms another. What should be examined?
questions.explanation: Different subgroup effects may matter for deployment even when an overall average looks favourable.

questions.prompt: Why can testing many outcome metrics create a problem?
options: It increases opportunities for chance findings
questions.explanation: A testing plan should account for multiple outcomes and distinguish primary from exploratory metrics.

questions.prompt: What is a business decision after finding a small positive effect?
options: Compare expected benefit, uncertainty and rollout cost
Reject automatically because the effect is not 100%
Implement automatically because p is small
questions.explanation: Statistical evidence is one input to a decision with practical costs and benefits.

questions.prompt: Why log exposure rather than only assignment?
options: Assigned users may never encounter the feature
Exposure proves the outcome is causal
Exposure and assignment are always identical
questions.explanation: Exposure records help diagnose delivery and interpret the experiment population.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is most vulnerable to seasonality confounding?
options: A balanced experiment with consistent measurement
Before-and-after results without a concurrent control
questions.explanation: Time changes can affect outcomes independently of the intervention.

questions.prompt: What is a difference-in-differences design's key identifying assumption?
questions.explanation: The design relies on comparable counterfactual trends in the absence of treatment.

questions.prompt: What does blocking before random assignment help achieve?
options: Eliminate the need for a control
Guarantee every treatment effect is positive
questions.explanation: Randomising within strata can improve balance and precision.

questions.prompt: Why document changes made during an experiment?
options: They can alter treatment or measurement interpretation
questions.explanation: Mid-test changes can make early and late observations reflect different conditions.

questions.prompt: What should a final experiment report include?
options: Design, sample sizes, effects, uncertainty and limitations
questions.explanation: A complete report makes the evidence and its limits reviewable.

questions.prompt: What is data leakage?
options: Using information unavailable at prediction time or from held-out data
questions.explanation: Leakage makes evaluation unrealistically optimistic by supplying inappropriate information.

questions.prompt: Which feature is leakage when predicting loan default at application time?
questions.explanation: A later collections outcome is unavailable when the application prediction is made.

questions.prompt: Why split data before fitting an imputer?
options: To make the dataset smaller permanently
To guarantee zero missing values in future data
To prevent held-out values influencing learned preprocessing
To force the median to zero
questions.explanation: Imputation statistics should be estimated from training data only.

questions.prompt: Where should feature selection be fitted during cross-validation?
options: After combining train and validation labels
Only on the final test labels
Once on the entire dataset before CV
questions.explanation: Selection using held-out labels leaks information into the evaluation.

questions.prompt: What does a preprocessing pipeline help enforce?
options: Consistent fitting and transformation across splits
A fixed number of features forever
questions.explanation: Pipelines keep preprocessing steps coupled to model training and evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a validation set?
options: Provide the final untouched evaluation after every choice
questions.explanation: Validation data guide choices; a separate test set can assess the resulting process.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an untouched test set?
options: Select the best feature by test correlation
Estimate performance after model choices are fixed
questions.explanation: Repeatedly using the test set for choices makes it part of model development.

questions.prompt: Why can a random split be inappropriate for forecasting?
options: Random splits always create duplicate timestamps
It may mix future information into past prediction tasks
questions.explanation: A chronological evaluation better matches predicting future observations.

questions.prompt: When is group-aware splitting needed?
options: Only when the target is numeric
When related rows from the same entity must stay together
Whenever a column is alphabetically sorted
questions.explanation: Entity overlap can make validation unrealistically easy when within-entity observations are similar.

questions.prompt: Why keep one patient's records in a single split?
options: To evaluate generalisation to unseen patients without identity leakage
questions.explanation: Shared patient-specific patterns can leak across ordinary row splits.

questions.prompt: What does stratified splitting try to preserve?
options: The exact order of all rows
The value of every feature mean
questions.explanation: Stratification helps maintain representation of target classes.

questions.prompt: What is one-hot encoding?
options: Sorting category labels by frequency only
Assigning arbitrary continuous distances to categories
Replacing all categories with the global mean always
questions.explanation: Each indicator marks membership in a category.

questions.prompt: Why can integer labels be misleading for unordered categories?
options: They can imply an artificial order or distance
They force every model to be nonlinear
Integers cannot represent labels at all
questions.explanation: Some models interpret numerical codes as ordered magnitudes.

questions.prompt: What is ordinal encoding appropriate for?
options: Arbitrary postal codes as continuous quantities
questions.explanation: The encoding should reflect a real ordering in the category meaning.

questions.prompt: Why plan for unseen categories at inference?
options: Unseen categories automatically become correct predictions
Training always contains every possible value
New inputs may contain labels absent during training
questions.explanation: An explicit unknown-category policy prevents failures or inconsistent encoding.

questions.prompt: What does standardisation commonly do?
options: Subtract the training mean and divide by training standard deviation
Replace every value with its rank
Force every variable to be normally distributed
questions.explanation: Standardisation changes location and scale but does not guarantee a normal shape.

questions.prompt: Does standard scaling make a skewed distribution normal?
options: Only if the mean is positive
questions.explanation: A linear rescaling preserves the distribution's shape.

questions.prompt: Which method is especially sensitive to feature scale?
options: A decision tree using ordered split thresholds
A rule that predicts the majority class
questions.explanation: Distance calculations can be dominated by features with larger numerical ranges.

questions.prompt: Why are decision-tree splits often less sensitive to simple positive linear scaling?
options: They depend on feature order and thresholds
questions.explanation: A monotonic linear rescaling preserves the ordering available for split decisions.

questions.prompt: What does min-max scaling typically use?
questions.explanation: The fitted range determines the transformation applied to later values.

questions.prompt: Can new values fall outside the usual 0–1 range after min-max scaling?
options: Only if all training values are zero
Yes, if they exceed the training range
questions.explanation: The fitted scaling does not necessarily clip new extreme observations.

questions.prompt: What is a potential benefit of log-transforming positive skewed values?
options: Guaranteeing better performance for every model
questions.explanation: A logarithm reduces the relative spacing of large positive values.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before applying a logarithm?
options: Only whether the column name is short
Whether values are in the transformation's domain
Whether the model is a classifier
questions.explanation: An ordinary real-valued logarithm requires positive inputs.

questions.prompt: Why add a missingness indicator in some settings?
options: It restores the true missing value
It makes imputation unnecessary for every model
Missingness itself may carry useful information
It guarantees missing values are random
questions.explanation: A flag can help the model distinguish observed values from imputed ones.

questions.prompt: What is target encoding's leakage risk?
options: Category statistics may include a row's own target or held-out labels
It always removes the target column
questions.explanation: Target-derived encodings need training-only and often out-of-fold construction.

questions.prompt: What is out-of-fold target encoding?
options: Using the final test target for every row
Encoding each row with its own target
Encoding a row using target statistics from other folds
questions.explanation: Excluding the row's fold reduces direct target leakage into its encoded feature.

questions.prompt: Why remove exact cross-split duplicates when evaluating generalisation?
options: They can let a model effectively see evaluation cases during training
They are required for every cross-validation scheme
questions.explanation: Repeated cases across splits can inflate apparent generalisation performance.

questions.prompt: What is a high-cardinality categorical feature?
options: A feature with exactly two values
A feature with a large numerical mean only
A feature with no missing data
A feature with many distinct categories
questions.explanation: High cardinality refers to the number of distinct category values.

questions.prompt: Why can raw user IDs be risky model features?
options: They may encourage memorisation rather than transferable patterns
questions.explanation: Identifier-based patterns may not generalise to unseen users.

questions.prompt: What are interaction features intended to represent?
options: Only the marginal mean of one feature
questions.explanation: An interaction allows the influence of one variable to depend on another.

questions.prompt: Why include cyclical encodings for hour of day?
options: To rank hours by importance automatically
questions.explanation: Sine and cosine representations can preserve the wraparound structure.

questions.prompt: What is a rolling feature's forecasting requirement?
options: Compute the window over the full future period
Include future observations for smoother results
Use only information available before the prediction cutoff
questions.explanation: Features must obey the information boundary of the real prediction task.

questions.prompt: What is train-serving skew?
options: A mismatch between training and inference data processing
The difference between CPU brands alone
questions.explanation: Inconsistent feature construction can degrade deployed predictions.

questions.prompt: Why save fitted preprocessing with the model?
options: Inference must reuse the learned transformations
It eliminates the need for input validation
The model otherwise changes every label randomly
questions.explanation: The same fitted encoding, scaling and imputation should be used at prediction time.

questions.prompt: What should happen if a required input column is absent at inference?
options: Return a clear validation error or use an explicit designed fallback
Assume the missing value is always zero
questions.explanation: A defined input contract prevents unnoticed feature mismatches.

questions.prompt: What is nested cross-validation useful for?
options: Separating hyperparameter selection from performance estimation
Using test labels in every training fold
questions.explanation: An inner loop selects settings and an outer loop estimates the selection process's performance.

questions.prompt: Why does resampling imbalanced data belong inside training folds?
options: To avoid leaking synthetic or duplicated information into validation
To remove minority cases from testing
questions.explanation: Oversampling before splitting can contaminate validation with training-related observations.

questions.prompt: What makes a feature useful for deployment?
options: It is expensive even when irrelevant
It has the strongest full-data target correlation regardless of timing
It is informative and available reliably at prediction time
questions.explanation: Predictive value must be paired with feasible and leakage-free availability.

questions.prompt: What is supervised learning?
options: Learning from examples with target labels
Clustering with no targets in every case
questions.explanation: Supervised models use paired inputs and outcomes to learn a prediction rule.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes regression from classification?
options: Regression predicts a numeric quantity; classification predicts a class
questions.explanation: The target type determines the task distinction.

questions.prompt: Which task is a classification problem?
options: Predicting whether a payment is fraudulent
questions.explanation: Fraud status is a categorical outcome.

questions.prompt: Which task is a regression problem?
questions.explanation: Delivery duration is a numeric quantity.

questions.prompt: What does a majority-class baseline predict?
options: The most frequent training class for every case
The least frequent class for every case
The true label using test data
questions.explanation: This baseline shows what class imbalance alone can achieve.

questions.prompt: What is a simple squared-error regression baseline?
questions.explanation: The mean minimises training squared error among constant predictions.

questions.prompt: What does overfitting usually look like?
options: Identical perfect performance in every setting
Poor performance caused only by too few columns
A model with no fitted parameters
Strong training performance but weaker unseen-data performance
questions.explanation: An overfit model learns sample-specific patterns that do not generalise well.

questions.prompt: What does underfitting indicate?
options: The model has memorised every training case
The model fails to capture important training patterns
The model is always too large
The test set was necessarily leaked
questions.explanation: An overly restrictive or poorly trained model can miss useful structure.

questions.prompt: What does regularisation generally discourage?
options: Excessive model complexity under a chosen penalty
questions.explanation: A penalty can reduce overly flexible fitting and improve generalisation.

questions.prompt: What is a hyperparameter?
options: A setting chosen outside the ordinary parameter-fitting step
questions.explanation: Examples include tree depth, neighbour count and regularisation strength.

questions.prompt: Which parameter is a decision-tree hyperparameter?
options: A split threshold learned during fitting
A leaf prediction learned from data
questions.explanation: Maximum depth is typically selected before fitting a tree.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of a learning curve?
options: Compare performance as training-data size changes
questions.explanation: Learning curves help diagnose data limitations and fitting behaviour.

questions.prompt: What does linear regression model in its basic form?
options: The exact causal effect of every feature
A linear combination of input features
questions.explanation: The predicted outcome is expressed through an intercept and weighted features.

questions.prompt: Why can a linear model still use polynomial features?
options: It can be linear in coefficients while nonlinear in original inputs
questions.explanation: Linearity refers to how coefficients enter the model.

questions.prompt: What does logistic regression commonly estimate for binary classification?
questions.explanation: A logistic link maps a linear score to a probability between zero and one.

questions.prompt: What does a decision tree use to form predictions?
options: A fixed alphabetical ordering of labels
Only a global average in every leafless case
questions.explanation: Trees partition the feature space and predict from terminal regions.

questions.prompt: What can increasing tree depth do?
questions.explanation: Deeper trees can represent more detailed patterns, including noise.

questions.prompt: What is a random forest?
options: An ensemble of randomised decision trees
questions.explanation: Forests combine trees trained with randomness in observations and/or feature selection.

questions.prompt: What is bagging intended to reduce for unstable learners?
questions.explanation: Averaging models fitted to resampled data can stabilise predictions.

questions.prompt: How does boosting typically build an ensemble?
options: Sorting labels and returning the first
Sequentially adding learners to improve the current model
Replacing validation with a single chart
Training one fixed model without updates
questions.explanation: Boosting adds models in a sequence that addresses the current objective or errors.

questions.prompt: What is a boosting learning rate used for?
options: Setting the number of input columns
Changing the target's physical unit automatically
questions.explanation: A smaller learning rate reduces each stage's update size.

questions.prompt: What does k-nearest neighbours use at prediction time?
options: Nearby training examples under a distance measure
Only the most recent SQL query
questions.explanation: KNN uses local neighbours to infer a class or value.

questions.prompt: What can a very small k in KNN cause?
options: A constant prediction for every input
Sensitivity to noise in nearby points
questions.explanation: Small neighbourhoods can make predictions depend strongly on individual observations.

questions.prompt: What can a very large k in KNN cause?
options: Overly smooth predictions that miss local structure
Perfect memorisation of every training label
questions.explanation: Large neighbourhoods average over broader regions and may underfit local patterns.

questions.prompt: What is the curse of dimensionality relevant to KNN?
options: Distances can become less informative in many dimensions
All features become equal to zero
The number of classes must double
questions.explanation: High-dimensional space can make local neighbourhoods sparse and less discriminative.

questions.prompt: What is the objective of k-means clustering?
options: Reduce within-cluster squared distances to centroids
Maximise classification accuracy against unseen labels automatically
Force clusters to have equal populations
questions.explanation: K-means assigns points to minimise within-cluster squared Euclidean dispersion.

questions.prompt: Why does k-means usually need feature scaling?
options: Scaling guarantees the correct number of clusters
It requires all features to be probabilities
questions.explanation: The distance objective depends on the numerical scales of the inputs.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of k-means for irregularly shaped clusters?
options: It cannot use more than two observations
It always identifies arbitrary shapes perfectly
Centroid-based partitions may not match those shapes
questions.explanation: K-means favours compact distance-based clusters rather than arbitrary density shapes.

questions.prompt: Which clustering method can label sparse points as noise?
questions.explanation: DBSCAN uses density connectivity and can leave points outside clusters.

questions.prompt: What does PCA seek in its leading components?
options: Directions of greatest variance under its formulation
Directions maximising a target label by default
One component for each class automatically
questions.explanation: PCA is an unsupervised projection based on variance structure.

questions.prompt: Why may PCA components be difficult to interpret?
options: They keep all original feature names unchanged
They always contain only one nonzero loading
questions.explanation: A component is a weighted combination that may not map to one familiar concept.

questions.prompt: What does gradient descent update?
options: Parameters in a direction that reduces the objective locally
questions.explanation: Gradient descent moves parameters against the gradient of the objective.

questions.prompt: What can an excessively large learning rate cause?
questions.explanation: Large updates can overshoot useful parameter regions.

questions.prompt: What is a mini-batch?
options: A set containing only test labels
A subset used for one training update
questions.explanation: Mini-batch training estimates updates from a subset of training examples.

questions.prompt: What does an epoch represent?
options: One pass through the training data
questions.explanation: An epoch refers to a complete traversal of the training examples.

questions.prompt: What does early stopping monitor to limit training?
options: Only the final test labels after every batch
Only the number of chart colours
questions.explanation: Stopping when validation improvement stalls can help control overfitting.

questions.prompt: Why keep the final test set out of early stopping?
options: Early stopping never affects the model
Test data cannot be read by computers
questions.explanation: Using test results to choose the stopping point leaks evaluation information into training.

questions.prompt: What does dropout do during neural-network training?
options: Randomly disables selected activations according to its rule
questions.explanation: Dropout introduces training-time randomness as a regularisation technique.

questions.prompt: What do nonlinear activation functions enable?
options: Neural networks to represent nonlinear relationships
questions.explanation: Composing only linear layers remains a linear transformation without nonlinear activations.

questions.prompt: What is transfer learning?
options: Reusing representations or weights learned on another task or dataset
questions.explanation: A pretrained model can provide useful starting representations for a related problem.

questions.prompt: What is fine-tuning?
options: Updating pretrained model parameters for a target task
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning adapts existing weights using additional task-specific training.

questions.prompt: Why compare a complex model with a simple baseline?
options: To remove uncertainty from every result
To guarantee the complex model wins
To establish whether complexity provides useful improvement
questions.explanation: A baseline quantifies the value gained from added modelling effort.

questions.prompt: What is a reproducible model comparison?
options: Only the best training score reported
Metrics selected after seeing each model's result
Candidates evaluated on consistent splits and metrics
Each candidate tested on a different convenient dataset
questions.explanation: Consistent evaluation makes performance differences more interpretable.

questions.prompt: Why record random seeds?
options: To make stochastic steps easier to reproduce
To prove a model is fair
To guarantee identical results on every hardware stack
questions.explanation: Seeds control random choices, though full reproducibility can require additional environment controls.

questions.prompt: What is a model ensemble?
options: A combination of predictions from multiple models
questions.explanation: Ensembles aggregate models to exploit complementary behaviour.

questions.prompt: When might a simpler model be preferable despite a slightly lower score?
options: Only when the dataset has no rows
When interpretability, latency or maintenance benefits outweigh the difference
questions.explanation: Deployment decisions include practical constraints beyond one evaluation metric.

questions.prompt: What does a model's decision threshold control in binary classification?
options: How scores are converted into class decisions
The number of features in every model
How the original labels were collected
questions.explanation: Threshold choice changes which predicted probabilities are classified as positive.

questions.prompt: Why should threshold selection use validation data and business costs?
options: The test set should be repeatedly optimised
The default threshold is always optimal
questions.explanation: A useful threshold reflects the task's trade-offs without contaminating final evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is a true positive in fraud detection?
options: A legitimate case flagged as fraud
A fraudulent case correctly flagged as fraud
questions.explanation: A true positive has a positive actual label and a positive prediction.

questions.prompt: What is a false positive in fraud detection?
options: A legitimate case incorrectly flagged as fraud
questions.explanation: A false positive flags a case whose actual label is negative.

questions.prompt: What is a false negative in disease screening?
options: A healthy person classified as positive
A diseased person classified as negative
A diseased person classified as positive
A healthy person classified as negative
questions.explanation: A false negative misses a genuinely positive case.

questions.prompt: How is precision calculated?
questions.explanation: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are truly positive.

questions.prompt: How is recall calculated?
questions.explanation: Recall is the share of actual positive cases detected by the model.

questions.prompt: A model flags 20 cases, of which 15 are truly positive. What is precision?
questions.explanation: Precision is 15 divided by 20, or 75%.

questions.prompt: There are 40 actual positive cases and the model detects 30. What is recall?
questions.explanation: Recall is 30 divided by 40, or 75%.

questions.prompt: What is specificity?
questions.explanation: Specificity is the proportion of actual negatives correctly classified.

questions.prompt: What does the F1 score combine?
options: Training loss and test loss through their difference
Specificity and data size through their product
Precision and recall through their harmonic mean
Accuracy and runtime through their sum
questions.explanation: F1 balances precision and recall and is low when either is low.

questions.prompt: Why can 99% accuracy be weak evidence with 1% positives?
options: Predicting every case negative already gives 99% accuracy
questions.explanation: A majority-class prediction can hide complete failure to detect positives.

questions.prompt: For fixed scores, what typically happens to positive predictions when the threshold is lowered?
options: There are at least as many positive predictions
questions.explanation: Lowering the cutoff admits additional cases as positive.

questions.prompt: What does a ROC curve plot?
options: True-positive rate against false-positive rate across thresholds
Training loss against calendar date only
questions.explanation: ROC curves compare sensitivity and false-positive rate as the threshold varies.

questions.prompt: Why inspect a precision-recall curve for rare-positive tasks?
options: It focuses on positive detection and false-alarm burden
questions.explanation: Precision and recall expose trade-offs that can be obscured by a large negative class.

questions.prompt: What does probability calibration assess?
options: Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies
Whether the model uses a GPU
Whether every class decision is correct
questions.explanation: Among cases given similar probabilities, event frequencies should be consistent with those probabilities.

questions.prompt: A well-calibrated model assigns 0.8 to many comparable cases. Approximately what should happen?
options: About 80% should be positive over a sufficiently large group
questions.explanation: Calibration is a frequency statement across groups of probabilistic predictions.

questions.prompt: What does MAE average?
questions.explanation: MAE averages the magnitudes of residuals in the target's units.

questions.prompt: What does RMSE do compared with MAE?
options: Penalises large errors more strongly through squaring
Returns a percentage in every case
questions.explanation: Squaring makes large residuals contribute disproportionately before taking the square root.

questions.prompt: For absolute errors 2, 4 and 6, what is MAE?
questions.explanation: The average absolute error is (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4.

questions.prompt: What is a problem with MAPE when actual values are zero?
options: Its ordinary formula divides by zero
It no longer depends on predictions
questions.explanation: Percentage error requires division by the actual value, which fails at zero without special handling.

questions.prompt: Can R-squared be negative on held-out data?
options: No, it is always between zero and one
Yes, if predictions are worse than the constant-mean benchmark used by the metric
Only when all predictions are exact
questions.explanation: A model can have larger squared error than the reference constant prediction.

questions.prompt: What can patterned residuals suggest?
questions.explanation: Residual patterns can reveal unmodelled relationships or assumptions that fail.

questions.prompt: Why inspect errors by subgroup?
options: Overall averages can hide uneven performance
Every subgroup must have identical labels
questions.explanation: Different populations may experience different error rates or error costs.

questions.prompt: Why include subgroup sample sizes with metrics?
options: All subgroup scores are equally stable
Small groups can have uncertain estimates
questions.explanation: Precision of subgroup estimates depends on the amount of supporting data.

questions.prompt: What does permutation importance measure?
options: The performance change when a feature's values are shuffled
The raw number of categories only

questions.prompt: Why can correlated features complicate importance scores?

questions.prompt: What is a local explanation intended to describe?

questions.prompt: What is data drift?
options: A change in the input-data distribution
A guaranteed change in the target relationship only
questions.explanation: Data drift refers to changing feature distributions relative to a reference period.

questions.prompt: What is concept drift?
options: A change in the number of report pages
A change in the relationship between inputs and the target
questions.explanation: A previously learned mapping may become less suitable when the target relationship changes.

questions.prompt: Why monitor deployed performance when labels become available?

questions.prompt: What should a model card describe?

questions.prompt: What is a useful error-analysis practice?

Change the test labels to match predictions
Inspect only correctly predicted easy cases

questions.prompt: Why evaluate latency alongside accuracy for a live service?
options: Accuracy becomes irrelevant for all services

A random change in the file name

questions.prompt: What should a project README explain first?
options: Only a list of every library
Only the installation of unrelated tools
The problem and why it matters

questions.prompt: What makes a reported project finding credible?
options: A traceable calculation or visual supporting it
A screenshot with no data source
A claim that every company would benefit
questions.explanation: Findings should connect to reproducible evidence rather than unsupported impact claims.

questions.prompt: Why record the dataset source and licence?
options: To guarantee the dataset is unbiased
To support attribution and permitted reuse
To prove the model will generalise

questions.prompt: What belongs in reproducibility instructions?
options: Environment requirements and exact run steps
Only a list of personal interests
Only a screenshot of the final chart
questions.explanation: Another person should be able to set up and run the workflow.

questions.prompt: Why pin or record dependency versions?
options: It makes every dependency permanently secure
It removes the need for source code
questions.explanation: Version information helps recreate the environment used for the results.

questions.prompt: What should be excluded from a public project repository?
options: Real credentials and private personal data

questions.prompt: What is a useful example environment file?
options: A private access token in plain text
Placeholder variable names without real secrets
A database export with user details
questions.explanation: An example file documents configuration while keeping sensitive values out of source control.

questions.prompt: Why separate raw data from processed outputs?
options: To make transformations and provenance traceable
To guarantee the raw data have no errors

questions.prompt: How should a portfolio describe an estimated revenue opportunity?
options: As an estimate with assumptions and limits

As realised revenue without implementation evidence

questions.prompt: What is a strong project conclusion?
options: Claim the model solves every future case
Answer the original question and state limitations
questions.explanation: A conclusion should connect the work to the question and its evidential limits.

questions.prompt: What is a useful limitation to disclose?
options: The dataset covers one region and may not generalise elsewhere
The repository has a short name
The chart uses a green accent
questions.explanation: Coverage restrictions affect how broadly findings can be applied.

questions.prompt: What should a portfolio dashboard link be accompanied by?
options: A claim that filters never change results
A private password in the README
questions.explanation: Context helps reviewers interpret and assess the dashboard correctly.

questions.prompt: Why include a simple baseline in a machine-learning portfolio?
options: To show whether the proposed model adds value
To guarantee the final model wins
questions.explanation: A baseline anchors the reported improvement to a meaningful reference.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate project milestone?
options: An indefinite goal to become perfect
A verifiable deliverable such as a validated cleaning report
questions.explanation: Concrete deliverables make progress and review criteria observable.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer be able to trace from a headline result?

questions.prompt: Why include tests for critical data transformations?
options: To prove every business conclusion is causal
To catch changes that break important assumptions
questions.explanation: Checks on keys, totals and expected outputs help prevent silent regressions.

questions.prompt: What demonstrates technical judgement in an interview project walkthrough?
options: Reading the README without explaining choices
Naming as many frameworks as possible
Explaining trade-offs, failed approaches and evidence for decisions
questions.explanation: Reasoned decisions and honest evaluation show understanding beyond implementation.

exercises.title: Revenue by customer
exercises.prompt: Given orders(customer_id, amount, status), return total paid revenue by customer, highest first. Exclude unpaid orders.
exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
exercises.explanation: Filter paid rows before aggregating. Group by customer and order by the computed sum.
